newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE accuses Bosnian Serbs of electoral abuses.
newsitem.headline: OSCE accuses Bosnian Serbs of electoral abuses.

text.p: International monitors on Monday accused Bosnian Serb authorities of fraudulently registering voters in a bid to manipulate forthcoming municipal elections.

Monitors for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) found widespread abuses by Bosnian Serb authorities which amounted to an attempt to orchestrate "massive fraud," said an internal OSCE report obtained by Reuters.
The report from the OSCE office in the Serb-controlled town of Banja Luka said the abuses cast serious doubt on the commitment of Serb authorities to hold free and fair elections.

"That this fraud is so blatantly conducted at a number of registration centres illustrates the contempt with which the Republika Srpska (Serb republic authorities) view any attempt to run democratic elections and, presumably, also any penalties to be paid for non-compliance," the report said.
Evidence of fraud emerged two weeks after voter registration began across Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat territories under OSCE supervision.

The registration process, which started on May 5, is due to last six weeks and is supposed to provide a reliable list of voters for future elections in Bosnia. The municipal polls are scheduled for September.

The report said that Serb authorities were trying to inflate the number of eligible Serb voters in western areas of Serb-held territory, where tens of thousands of Moslems were expelled during the 1992-1995 Bosnian war.
Serb officials were issuing forged citizenship papers to Serbs who fled Croatia in 1995 and resettled in Bosnia, the report said.
Serb authorities were also discouraging Serbs from voting in municipalities where they lived before the conflict which now lie inside the country's Moslem-Croat federation.

Bosnia's hotly-contested municipal polls were originally scheduled to coincide with parliamentary elections last September. The vote was postponed because of registration abuses which the OSCE again blamed mainly on Serb authorities.
Bosnian Serbs were accused of trying to seal the gains of "ethnic cleansing" by registering refugees in contested areas.
The local elections are viewed as a chance to help reunify the divided country by enabling Bosnians who were expelled or displaced to regain control over their pre-war townships.

An OSCE spokesman said any fraud that is identified will result in severe penalties, including disqualifying a political party in a municipality from running in elections or striking off candidates from election lists.
"We are looking extraordinarily carefully at all allegations that come to us about fraud," spokesman David Foley told reporters.
After last year's national elections were plagued by allegations of fraud and dubious voter lists, the OSCE drew up rules for registration devised to discourage manipulation of the refugee vote.

The rules allow refugees abroad to vote in municipalities where they "intend to live" if they submit documents proving a legal connection to the area before the war, such as property ownership or tenancy rights.
Displaced Bosnians who want to vote in towns where they have resettled must prove they moved to the area before August 1996.
